why: Three files, 1120 lines, and they are not one job but two. wa_decrypt.py (213 lines) reimplements the WhatsApp Desktop WebView2 key chain in Python: ODUID from clipc.dll, staticKey via DPAPI-NG NCryptProtectSecret (LOCAL=user), clientKey carved from session.db-wal with sha1(clientKey) asserted against the session directory name, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 plus AES-256-CBC to the nativeSettings key, then per-type keys over AES-OFB page-encrypted SQLite. wa_query.py (178 lines) is the part no prior art supplies: a contacts/stats/search/thread CLI over the decrypted store with name resolution and date filters, output shaped for an agent to quote from. wa_act.py (729 lines, two thirds of the component) is a different thing again, a CDP driver against live WhatsApp Web that exists because the decrypted linked-device store has no from-me flag and cannot attribute a line to a speaker. The decryption is genuinely prior art and this record says so; the CORPUS QUERY is what is not available anywhere as a tool, and that is a 178-line file. The honest reading of the size is that the component is 549 lines of automation wrapped around 178 lines of the actual capability. Rechecked 2026-08-07: the split still holds and wa_act.py is untouched by the cleanup fix below (729 lines, no diff against the prior commit), so the 549-vs-178 shape argument is unchanged.
what_ours_does: Decrypts to a local temp directory on a snapshot copy without touching the live store, works while WhatsApp is running via shared-mode reads, resolves chatIds to contact names, and answers a question with dated quotes plus a stated coverage window rather than a dump. States its own epistemic limits in SKILL.md: no sender direction in the store, no media, group prefixes only on @g.us, coverage is what the linked device synced.
strongest_counterargument: ZAPiXDESK already does the decryption, it was published first, it is GPLv3, it is the source this reimplementation cites, and it does one thing ours does not: it hashes the extraction for chain of custody. Reimplementing a published forensic technique in a second language is the textbook case of code that should have been a dependency. The counterargument goes further than the code: the ONLY reason the query half exists at all is that the decrypted output is a raw SQLite file, and a raw SQLite file is already queryable by sqlite3, so `wa_query.py` is arguably 178 lines of convenience over four SQL statements. Against that: ZAPiXDESK is a PowerShell script with C# and Bouncy Castle that produces a ZIP for a forensic suite to open, its stated dependency is possessing the ODUID, and it has no query surface at all. Shelling out to it would mean adding a .NET crypto dependency and a ZIP unpack step to get to the same SQLite file, on a machine where the Python path already works. That is a defensible reason to keep the 213 lines and a WEAK reason to keep the other 907. If wa_act.py were split out to its own component, this record's verdict would be closer to a coin flip. Rechecked 2026-08-07 against ZAPiXDESK's live repository: pushed_at is 2026-06-23, before the 2026-07-31 review, 0 GitHub releases, and its README still shows only an MD5 chain-of-custody hash and no query surface (VERIFIED, GitHub API + raw README fetch, this session). Upstream gained nothing in the interval; the counterargument is unchanged, not strengthened.

alternatives.name: ZAPiXDESK (kraftdenker / Alberto Magno)
alternatives.why_not: The closest prior art by a wide margin and the acknowledged source of the technique, cited in our own SKILL.md. It targets both WebView2 and legacy UWP builds, extracts the ODUID live, decrypts every LocalState db and WAL, and emits a ZIP with an MD5 for chain of custody, which is a capability ours lacks. Rejected as a dependency rather than as a technique: it is PowerShell plus C# over Bouncy Castle producing an archive for a forensic tool to open, and it never queries what it decrypts. Adopting it swaps a stdlib-plus-cryptography Python path for a .NET toolchain, and still leaves the entire query surface to build. Its MD5 manifest is worth stealing and is not in improvement_owed only because chain of custody is not this use case. Rechecked 2026-08-07 (VERIFIED, GitHub API): last push 2026-06-23T15:00:16Z (before the 2026-07-31 review), 0 releases, repo not archived, still GPLv3, 70 stars. `updated_at` shows 2026-08-02 but that is metadata churn (stars, traffic), not a content push; `pushed_at` is the honest signal and it is silent since June. README fetched fresh still reads 'MD5 HASH file is generates for chain-of-custody purposes' with no mention of query or search. Nothing changed: still worth stealing the hash idea, still no query surface to adopt instead of ours.

alternatives.name: Kim, Hur, Kang and Kim, 'Analyzing the Web and UWP versions of WhatsApp for digital forensics', FSI: Digital Investigation v52 (2025), art. 301861
alternatives.why_not: Not a tool, and listed because the record would be dishonest without it: this is the peer-reviewed reverse engineering the implementation stands on, covering WhatsApp Web v2.3000.x and UWP v2.2421.7.0 on Windows. A paper cannot be adopted, only implemented, which is what happened. Its relevance to the verdict is the reverse of an alternative: it means the key chain is published, will drift when WhatsApp changes it, and our 213 lines will need re-deriving from the next paper rather than from our own analysis. The publication also caps any novelty claim about the decryption to zero. Rechecked 2026-08-07 (VERIFIED, Crossref API): DOI 10.1016/j.fsidi.2024.301861 confirms the FSI:DI publication (2025-03), container-title 'Forensic Science International: Digital Investigation'. It is a formally published paper; nothing about it moves after publication. The SSRN mirror (10.2139/ssrn.4972794) is gated behind a Cloudflare challenge and could not be fetched directly this session; the Crossref record is sufficient since it is the record that matters (the journal DOI, not the preprint host).

alternatives.name: WhatsApp-Chat-Exporter (KnugiHK)
alternatives.why_not: The mature, maintained, cross-platform parser: Android msgstore including crypt12/14/15, iOS/iPadOS iTunes backups, HTML/JSON/text output, call logs, contacts, media organisation. It is better than ours at everything it covers, and it explicitly does not cover WhatsApp Desktop or Windows, which is the only store on this machine. Correct choice the day the operator wants the phone backup parsed; useless for the store that is actually here. Rechecked 2026-08-07 (VERIFIED, GitHub API + README fetch): actively maintained, pushed 2026-07-27, 1182 stars, latest tagged release still 0.13.0 (2026-01-24). Its own README's 'Windows' sections are about running the tool on Windows to parse Android/iOS backups, not about WhatsApp Desktop storage; grepping the fresh README for 'Desktop' and 'Windows' turns up zero mentions of the WebView2 store. Still does not cover the only store on this machine.

alternatives.name: Magnet AXIOM
alternatives.why_not: Industry-leading artifact coverage across mobile, computer, cloud and vehicle, with timeline analysis and reporting that would outclass any hand-rolled query. Rejected on shape and cost, not quality: it is a licensed investigator workstation aimed at law enforcement, federal and enterprise IR, priced accordingly, and its output is a case file and a report rather than a CLI an agent can call in a loop. Nothing in it is packageable into a skill that answers 'what did X say about Y in August' inside a session. Attempted recheck 2026-08-07: the product page is a JavaScript-rendered SPA and a static curl fetch returned 0 WhatsApp mentions in the raw HTML (NOT VERIFIED either way; no browser-rendering tool was available this session to confirm or refute WhatsApp Desktop coverage). Does not move the verdict, since AXIOM was rejected on shape and licensing cost, not on an unconfirmed capability gap.

alternatives.name: Belkasoft X Forensic
alternatives.why_not: Cheaper than AXIOM and perpetually licensed rather than term-based, which removes the usual objection to a commercial suite. Rejected for a specific reason found while reading it: its product page advertises WhatsApp support as cloud acquisition, backup download and QR-code chat download, and does not state WhatsApp DESKTOP WebView2 artifact support. The one capability needed is the one not confirmed, and buying a suite to find out is not a plan. Recheck this claim before any future purchase argument, since suite artifact coverage changes per release. Rechecked 2026-08-07 (VERIFIED, static fetch of belkasoft.com/x, text extracted from raw HTML): the WhatsApp line still reads exactly 'WhatsApp: backups downloading and QR code-based chat downloading', same two capabilities as the 2026-07-31 finding, still no stated WebView2/Desktop artifact support. The open question this record flagged stands unanswered in the same direction: still don't buy it to find out.

alternatives.name: The official WhatsApp Export Chat feature
alternatives.why_not: The simplest correct option and the one this record is obliged to compare against, since it needs no decryption, no reverse engineering and no maintenance. It is per-chat and manual, which is the disqualifier: the corpus question here spans every thread at once, and hand-exporting hundreds of chats to text files is not a corpus, it is a chore with a different failure mode. WhatsApp's own privacy policy confirms the relevant fact that makes the local path viable at all: messages are stored on the device and not typically on their servers, so there is no server-side archive to request instead. Attempted recheck 2026-08-07: the WhatsApp FAQ page returned 0 matches for 'export chat' in a static fetch (NOT VERIFIED either way; likely JS-rendered, no browser tool available). Does not move the verdict: the per-chat-manual limitation this record relies on is a product-shape fact unlikely to have changed, and the feature is rejected on scope (per-chat, not corpus-wide), not on an unconfirmed detail.

alternatives.name: sqlite3 against the decrypted file, with no query layer at all
alternatives.why_not: The other simplest option, and it is half-right. Once wa_decrypt.py has run, the store is an ordinary SQLite database and `message(rowid, id, chatId, timestamp, text)` is four joins away from every answer wa_query.py gives. What the 178 lines buy is name resolution (a chatId such as 53403707257078@lid is not a person), the busiest-thread tie-break on ambiguous names, and a fixed output shape that keeps other people's messages from being dumped wholesale into a model's context. That last one is a policy control, not a convenience, which is why the layer stays. No recheck needed: this alternative is the Python stdlib, not a moving target.

improvement_owed: PRIMARY DEFECT CLOSED 2026-08-07, commit f88d3a3 on this branch (lane-a/waived-domains-are-not-unmeasured), deployed to ~/.claude/skills/whatsapp-query (VERIFIED: wa_decrypt.py, wa_query.py and the new wa_store.py are byte-identical between the repo and the live skill directory, diffed this session; live mtimes are 2026-08-07 23:47, matching the commit). The 2026-07-31 finding was that nothing anywhere removed the plaintext mirror wa_decrypt.py writes (rmtree/unlink/tempfile all absent). That is no longer true: a new wa_store.py (107 lines, pure Python, no Windows API) stamps the store when written, and wa_decrypt.py now purges any previous store before writing a new one and prints its own expiry. wa_query.py now deletes and refuses to read a store that is either older than the 1-hour TTL or carries no stamp at all (unstamped fails toward deletion, which is what makes every pre-fix store get swept up too). Both ends also take an explicit `purge` verb. tests/test_wa_store.py has 11 tests; VERIFIED this session: `python -m pytest tests/test_wa_store.py -v` is 11 passed. Also VERIFIED this session, beyond the isolated wa_store tests: `python -m py_compile` succeeds on all four files; `python wa_query.py contacts --limit 3` and `python wa_query.py purge` both run to completion on this Linux host with LOCALAPPDATA unset, exercising the real `import wa_store` wiring in wa_query.py (not just the module in isolation) and reproducing the exact behavior test_an_absent_store_is_not_expired predicts; and `python wa_decrypt.py` runs past its own `import wa_store` line and reaches `main()`, failing only on the expected `KeyError: 'LOCALAPPDATA'`, which shows the added import does not break the module even where the DPAPI-NG/ctypes.wintypes body of it cannot execute. My independent read: this closes the defect as it was specifically named. It does not make the store disappear on a timer; expiry is enforced only at the NEXT invocation of wa_decrypt.py or wa_query.py, on the way in. A session that runs one query and then never touches the skill again still leaves the plaintext mirror on disk indefinitely, same as before, just capped in size to one store instead of accumulating across runs. That is a narrower exposure than the 2026-07-31 defect (which had literally no cleanup path, ever), so the record's own flip condition ('if the cleanup defect is still unfixed at recheck, move to replace-or-delete') is not triggered and 'keep-ours' still holds, but 'closed' should not be read as 'the mirror never persists'; it is 'the mirror cannot silently persist past the next use of the tool, or past one hour if the operator walks away'. RESIDUAL, carried forward from 2026-07-31 and NOT touched by this commit: (1) ZAPiXDESK's MD5 extraction hash for chain of custody was named as worth adopting and still is not present in wa_decrypt.py; (2) the component still has no entry in tools/audit/mutate.py and no selftest for the parts that cannot run here, wa_decrypt.py's DPAPI-NG/WebView2 key chain and wa_query.py's SQLite reads and wa_act.py's CDP driver; the 11 new tests prove only the lifetime rules (stamp, age, expire, purge) and say so in their own module docstring, not that decryption works or that the store wa_decrypt.py writes is the one wa_query.py opens.
